data.question: What happens if the market falls 20% and technology drops a further 10%?
data.answer:
In this scenario the portfolio falls 25.3%, a loss of about $63,313 that leaves $186,687. A 20% market fall on its own accounts for 21.5%: the portfolio's beta is 1.08, so it moves slightly more than the market.

The extra 10% hit to technology adds the rest, because technology is 38% of the portfolio. NVDA is the largest single loss at $15,507. TLT is the only holding that gains, because its beta is negative (-0.21).

For scale, the worst fall in this simulated history was 30.0%, so the scenario is shallower than anything the history contains. The estimate is linear: it scales each holding by its beta and ignores how correlations shift in a real sell-off.

data.question: Where is the risk in this portfolio coming from?
data.answer:
The portfolio's volatility is 18.7% a year, against 15.7% for the SPY benchmark, and its beta of 1.08 means it tends to move a little more than the market does.

Most of that risk sits in one place. Technology is 38% of the money, and NVDA alone is 14% of the weight but 25.7% of the portfolio's variance. At the other end, TLT has a slightly negative risk share (-1.1%): it has tended to move against the rest, which dampens the swings.

The worst fall in this history was 30.0%, from 30 March 2022 to 4 August 2022, over 91 trading days. On an ordinary bad day, the 95% one-day value at risk is 1.7%, or about $4,259.

data.question: What would cutting technology to 20% of the portfolio do to its risk?
data.answer:
Technology is 38% of the portfolio today. Moving it to 20% and scaling every other holding up in proportion would mean trading 18% of the portfolio, about $45,000.

On this history, volatility would go from 18.7% to 17.1%, beta from 1.08 to 0.99, and the worst fall from 30.0% to 25.0%. The 95% one-day value at risk would move from 1.70% to 1.54%.

For context, a simulation of the current mix over 252 trading days (5,000 paths) ends with a loss in 19% of them. The middle outcome is a gain of 17.4% and the 5th-percentile outcome is a loss of 13.2%. None of this says which mix is better. It describes how the risk numbers would have differed.
